content: Medical education refers to the structured process of training individuals to become medical practitioners. This encompasses both the initial education required to qualify as a doctor and the subsequent advanced training, such as residency programs, that follow. The structure and content of medical education and training vary significantly across different countries and regions. A variety of teaching methodologies are employed in medical education, and this field remains an active area of research within educational sciences. Entry-level medical education programs are tertiary-level courses conducted at medical schools. Depending on the jurisdiction and the specific university, these programs may be designed for undergraduate entry (as is common in most of Europe, India, and China) or graduate entry (as is typical in the United States). The initial phase of medical training is generally undertaken at a medical school. Traditionally, this phase is divided into two distinct components: preclinical studies and clinical studies. Preclinical studies focus on foundational sciences, including anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, and pathology. Clinical studies, on the other hand, involve education in various domains of clinical medicine, such as internal medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, psychiatry, and surgery. However, there is a growing trend toward the adoption of systems-based curricula, which integrate learning across disciplines. Many institutions have embraced this approach. Additionally, there has been an increase in programs that combine medical training with research (e.g., MD-PhD programs) or management education (e.g., MD-MBA programs), though these integrated programs have faced criticism in some quarters. After completing entry-level training, newly graduated doctors are often required to undergo a period of supervised practice before they are granted full registration. This phase typically lasts for one year and is commonly referred to as an internship, provisional registration, or residency, depending on the jurisdiction. Further specialized training in a specific field of medicine may follow. In some regions, this specialized training begins immediately after the completion of entry-level education. In other jurisdictions, junior doctors are required to complete several years of generalist, non-specialized training before they are eligible to pursue specialization in a particular area of medicine.
